title: Harness grok & streaming decision workshop
summary: POC scoping focused on integrating HelioHealth customer scripts into Redwood's benchmark harness. Primary decisions: streaming vs. non-streaming modes for chat-heavy routing, workload sizing (peak vs steady-state), success criteria for latency and throughput, and an initial 2-week pilot timeline. Agreed actions: SE to produce adapter template, customer to supply 3 canonical scripts + dataset slice, AE to send pilot SOW and security questionnaire.
topics: Harness adapter pattern and example mapping
Streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for chat/assist workloads
Success criteria: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput targets, token cost budget
Telemetry and log artifacts required for acceptance
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-06 16:00 PT | Duration: ~62m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Anika (HelioHealth Lead ML Eng), Marcus (HelioHealth Platform), Sofia (HelioHealth PM)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro round, then Priya will walk through the harness integration options.
[00:18] Anika: Thanks. happy to be here. our main goal is to validate throughput for chat assist use case and understand streaming tail-latency under typical patient-conversation lengths.
[00:32] Priya: Great. quick agenda: adapter pattern for customer scripts, load profile modeling (ramp/spike/idle), streaming vs non-streaming exec, success criteria proposals, and timeline. any additions?
[00:45] Sofia: Also security checklist and what telemetry you need for our acceptance.
[00:52] Jordan: We'll cover that. ok, Priya you want to take the adapter slide?
[01:00] Priya: Sure. so in Redwood's harness we have two integration points: 1) a lightweight adapter (python) that transforms your client script calls into the harness's request envelope, and 2) a heavier proxy mode which can stream tokens back to your client. the adapter is usually easiest for customers that already have internal SDK calls.
[01:28] Marcus: Quick q — our current system uses a gRPC-based client with a custom backpressure layer. does the adapter support gRPC or is it HTTP only?
[01:38] Priya: Today the template is HTTP/REST, but we've done gRPC bridges — it's a small wrapper. caveat: streaming with gRPC has different semantics around flow control, so we'll want to test a small spike.
[01:58] Anika: when you say streaming semantics, do you mean the KV cache or the token stream? i heard something about KV cash earlier in docs so wanted to clarify.
[02:09] Priya: ha yeah transcription sometimes writes K V cash — I meant KV cache and token streaming behavior. streaming reduces perceived latency for users but can hurt throughput if your client issues many small requests.
[02:28] Jordan: can we show an example script mapping? like our simple chat script to harness format.
[02:35] Priya: (shares screen briefly) here's a short snippet: customer sends history + prompt, adapter compresses history, optional prefix caching, then hits the harness stub which funnels requests to the runtime. for non-streaming we accumulate tokens server-side and send full response. for streaming we flush partial chunks as they're produced.
[03:10] Marcus: that flush behavior — does it require per-request flush thresholds? or is it purely model-driven?
[03:18] Priya: both. runtime will emit as tokens are produced; adapter can buffer small chunks to meet your network MTU or client decoding expectations. we recommend a small batching window (20–40ms) for high QPS chat workloads.
[03:36] Anika: ok that helps. about our workload — roughly 60% chat sessions are short (<= 40 tokens), 30% medium (40–200 tokens), rest are long notes (200–1k tokens). peak concurrent sessions are about 1200, sustained around 420.
[03:56] Jordan: good, that's actionable. we'll model both steady and burst profiles. Priya, what would you recommend for initial harness mode?
[04:05] Priya: for HelioHealth's distribution I'd propose a mixed-mode POC: run 70% non-streaming for long note completion (better throughput/cost), 30% streaming for interactive chat to measure tail-latency. that maps well to your token histogram.
[04:22] Sofia: mixed-mode seems fine. what's the overhead of supporting both in the harness?
[04:27] Priya: minimal — adapter routes per-script or per-route. runtime needs to be configured with two target variants: streaming-enabled model instance and streaming-optimized batch instance. routing policy handled by harness config.
[04:43] Marcus: are there any model variants we should consider to reduce cost — quantized or smaller context models for short chats?
[04:51] Priya: yes, we can recommend a smaller 8-bit quantized policy for short chats. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and expected token-cost delta. we'll include that in the deliverables.
[05:05] Anika: success criteria — we want p50 < 120ms for interactive chat, p95 < 450ms, and p99 < 1.2s; throughput target is 800 qps sustained for the steady-state mix and ability to handle 2x spiky bursts for 5 minutes. cost per 1M tokens should not exceed our budget threshold but we'll share the budget offline.
[05:29] Jordan: sounds reasonable. we'll aim to model those SLOs in the harness. for the p99 tail we might need warm KV prefixes, pre-warmed instances, and cold-start mitigation.
[05:42] Priya: right. we'll run three benchmark scenarios: 1) steady-state warm, 2) burst ramp (2x sustained for 5m), 3) cold-start ramp test. for streaming we'll look at tail behavior separately since p99 can be dominated by network/serialization.
[06:04] Sofia: telemetry — we need request-level traces, token-level timing, and sample outputs for quality checks. what do you typically provide?
[06:13] Priya: harness emits per-request timing (enqueue, start-gen, first-byte, last-byte), token counts, model variant, instance id. we can also snapshot sample responses with a hashed patient id for privacy. logs can be S3 or pushed to your ingestion.
[06:30] Marcus: S3 transfer is easiest. we use privacy pipeline to scrub PHI — will you accept pre-scrubbed samples?
[06:36] Jordan: yes, pre-scrubbed is preferred. we'll sign an A/NDA for any raw sets.
[06:43] Anika: timeline — what do you need from us to start the 2-week pilot?
[06:48] Priya: ideal inputs: 1) three canonical scripts covering short chat, medium assist, and long note completion; 2) a representative dataset slice (~48–72 hours trace, pre-scrubbed); 3) a target SLA matrix (you gave the p50/p95/p99 numbers — we'll formalize); 4) access or a runbook for your gRPC endpoint if you want proxy mode.
[07:10] Marcus: we can provision an internal staging gRPC endpoint, but prefer adapter-first. we'll push the scripts and dataset by Monday.
[07:18] Jordan: good. AE logistics — we'll send a short SOW and pilot scope doc. can you confirm procurement timeline?
[07:25] Sofia: procurement needs to sign off by Oct 20 to meet an end-of-month pilot start.
[07:31] Jordan: we can aim for pilot start Oct 27 then.
[07:35] Priya: ok next let's talk about acceptance artifacts — what constitutes a passing run?
[07:40] Anika: passing means SLOs met during the steady-state run, less than 3% error/no-response, and acceptable model outputs as judged by our QA team on 100 sample transcripts.
[07:52] Priya: we'll create acceptance dashboards with token cost breakdown. also recommend synthetic user jitter to emulate mobile clients — that often surfaces tail cases.
[08:03] Marcus: about error conditions — if model fallback occurs (streaming to non-streaming fallback), do you capture that and retry semantics?
[08:12] Priya: yes harness logs fallback events with reasons (capacity, error, timeout). we can post-process to show how many requests hit fallback and the latency delta.
[08:23] Jordan: any compliance requirements we should be aware of? SOC 2 is a must for us; also we need SSO/SAML and audit logs since access to sample outputs will be limited.
[08:35] Priya: Redwood can provide SOC 2 Type II report, SAML SSO integration guide, and configurable audit log retention. we'll attach the security pack.
[08:45] Sofia: fine. what about encryption — do you support customer-managed keys?
[08:50] Priya: yes, KMS integration is available for Private and Dedicated; for Hosted we support envelope encryption and can discuss a Bring-Your-Key path for bigger commitments.
[09:01] Anika: one technical nit — our existing client does aggressive connection pooling. when we simulate the harness we want to re-use connections to avoid head-of-line issues. can the adapter handle persistent connections?
[09:12] Priya: adapter supports keep-alive and connection pools. we'll include an example config.
[09:20] Marcus: test matrix — what exact metrics will you provide after each run?
[09:26] Priya: per-run CSV: request id, model variant, instance id, enqueue time, start-gen, first-byte, last-byte, token count, errors, fallback flag. plus aggregated p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1000 tokens.
[09:40] Jordan: ok let's walk through the pilot cadence — week 0 prep (scripts + dataset + SOW), week 1 harness integration + dry runs, week 2 benchmark runs + analysis + acceptance. does that align?
[09:54] Sofia: yes, but can we add a short mid-week sync to triage infra issues?
[10:00] Jordan: absolutely — we'll schedule a 30m mid-pilot check on Day 4.
[10:06] Anika: question on streaming measurement — how do you measure perceived latency for streaming (first token or partial chunk)?
[10:13] Priya: we measure first-byte and also time-to-n tokens (e.g., t-to-10 tokens) for progressive rendering. that helps quantify UX.
[10:22] Marcus: and for cost modeling you give us both token and instance-hour economics?
[10:27] Priya: yes. token cost per 1k and per-instance-hour run-rate, plus estimate of batch efficiency gains for non-streaming.
[10:35] Anika: what about load shaping — do you recommend synthetic users or replaying traces?
[10:40] Priya: both. we prefer to do a trace-driven replay for fidelity, with synthesized jitter and connection churn layered on top.
[10:48] Jordan: let's capture agreed inputs and owners now.
[10:52] Anika: owner: Helio to deliver three canonical scripts + pre-scrubbed dataset slice by 2026-10-11.
[10:59] Marcus: owner: Helio infra to stand up a staging endpoint or provide runbook by 2026-10-11.
[11:05] Priya: owner: Redwood SE to provide adapter template, example configs, and draft benchmark plan by 2026-10-13.
[11:13] Jordan: owner: AE to share SOW and security pack by 2026-10-08.
[11:19] Sofia: procurement to confirm by 2026-10-20.
[11:24] Priya: any red flags on streaming right now? I think main risk is many tiny requests causing overhead; we'll measure qps per connection to detect that.
[11:34] Anika: sounds ok. one risk is our long completion distribution — a small percent of 800-token notes could skew resource usage. how do you protect the pilot from being dominated by outliers?
[11:45] Priya: we'll cap concurrency per-session and use admission control with backpressure to preserve overall SLOs; long notes go to non-streaming pool.
[11:53] Jordan: ok let's recap next steps and schedule.
[12:00] Jordan: recap: Helio delivers scripts + dataset + staging runbook by Oct 11; Redwood SE delivers adapter template + benchmark plan by Oct 13; AE sends SOW + security pack by Oct 8; mid-pilot sync scheduled Day 4; pilot start target Oct 27.
[12:21] Sofia: confirmed. one ask — can you include a short how-to for local harness dry run so our engineers can iterate before you run the benchmark?
[12:30] Priya: yes, we'll include a dockerized local harness dev flow and example docker-compose for small-scale replay.
[12:38] Anika: great, thanks. that's all from us.
[12:41] Jordan: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs and SOW.
[12:45] (meeting ends)

Helio to deliver 3 scripts + pre-scrubbed dataset by 2026-10-11
Priya to deliver adapter template and benchmark plan by 2026-10-13
